content.problem: A model passed review last week. Someone changed its preprocessing or image today and reused the old approval. Bind review to the exact release bundle, load the selected artifact through a consumer, observe activation and rollback predictions, then practice retirement without losing the audit trail.
content.idea: Model governance connects ownership, evaluation, approval and lifecycle transitions. This local single-writer demonstration uses content-addressed bundle identities and a consumer that loads the selected model artifact. It exercises approval, activation, rollback, cache/reload and tombstone eligibility; it does not authenticate people or emulate a production registry.
objectives: Bind review and audit to immutable bundle identity
Observe consumer predictions before activation, after activation and after rollback
Reject invalid transitions without changing selection or behavior
Define active, fallback, cached and retired artifact eligibility

sections.title: Approval applies to a specific release
sections.body: Imagine the reviewed release is bundle A, with a specific model artifact, evaluation record, owner and target. If its weights or tokenizer change, the new bundle has a different identity, so the old approval cannot be carried over by keeping the same display name. In the fixture, approval is valid at time \(199\) and expired at times \(200\) and \(201\). The lifecycle checks also reject a stale approval, a wrong target and a version mismatch. Start each activation decision by checking which exact bundle was reviewed, whether the approval is still valid, and whether it covers this target. The bars summarize those decisions; the stored state explains why each attempt succeeded or failed.

check.prompt: Does changing a display name require the same response as changing weights?
check.answer: Not necessarily. Define which identities and semantics the policy binds. A cosmetic label and a changed numerical artifact are different events, and the policy should distinguish them explicitly.

sections.title: Inventory the complete release
sections.body: A release inventory is the set of facts a reviewer needs to know what will be served: model artifact and hash, evaluation identity, serving image, preprocessing or signature, precision, intended target and responsible owner. This fixture binds version, artifact hash, evaluation identity, owner, target and passing result. If any bound field changes, the release should be treated as a different object for approval. A real inventory should also make its code and preprocessing versions, limitations, dependency or license obligations and owner contact findable. A registry tag helps locate a release, but it does not enforce who may approve or activate it.

sections.title: Bind review to immutable evidence
sections.body: The approval check is a conjunction: the presented bundle must match the reviewed bundle, the approval must still be unexpired, and the requested target must be allowed. The execution checks validity at \(199\), \(200\) and \(201\) and prints true, false, false, making the expiry boundary visible. The recorded reviewer string is just a fixture value; it does not prove that the named person authenticated or had authority. In a real workflow, trusted identity, authorization and protected audit records must supply that evidence. A matching hash proves the bytes match the reviewed bytes, not that those bytes are useful or safe.

sections.title: Make failed transitions leave no side effects
sections.body: For each rejected transition, compare state before and after the attempt. The fixture tries stale, expired, wrong-target and mismatched-version activations, then verifies that the active pointer, consumer cache and prediction are unchanged. It also changes the bytes on disk and corrupts a cached artifact; both are rejected before prediction or cache mutation. This is the key failure-handling rule: validate the requested transition and artifact identity before committing any state change. In a real service, record the rejection reason and actor, and check the served output as well as the pointer so a failed activation cannot leave a half-updated consumer.

sections.title: Separate selection, rollout and monitoring
sections.body: Selection, rollout and monitoring answer separate questions. The registry selection chooses the approved version; rollout determines which serving processes or traffic use it; monitoring checks what those processes actually loaded and how they behave. In the local run, selecting B changes the consumer's prediction for \(x=1\) from \(3.0\) to \(3.4\). A deployment should confirm that serving processes report B's identity after rollout, then watch quality and service signals. A canary exposes a candidate to limited live traffic, while shadow traffic runs it without using its answer. Decide traffic assignment and stop conditions before interpreting a favorable curve.

sections.title: Rollback needs its own valid target
sections.body: A rollback is itself an activation decision, so its target must still be eligible. The fixture rolls from B back to A and the consumer prediction at \(x=1\) returns from \(3.4\) to \(3.0\). It rejects missing, retired, unapproved, changed-byte or incompatible targets before switching. Retirement writes a tombstone but retains the bundle and audit record; it removes eligibility for future selection. Because the active and fallback versions are protected, the operator first chooses a replacement and explicitly clears fallback eligibility before retiring them. Verify that the rollback target is still approved and eligible before changing selection, then confirm the consumer's result.

sections.title: Work through approval and lifecycle decisions
sections.body: For a lifecycle decision, name the release currently selected, the proposed transition and the evidence that would make you stop. If the activation is expired or targets a different bundle, reject it and confirm that pointer, cache and consumer output are unchanged. If rolling back, first verify that the proposed target remains approved and is neither retired nor byte-mismatched. After retirement, check that tombstones prevent future activation while the audit evidence remains available. The reviewer string in this fixture is not authentication, so a real process must establish the actor's identity and authority separately.

commands.label: Run the local ModelOps lifecycle experiment
commands.code: Save the lesson experiment as modelops_lifecycle.py and run: python modelops_lifecycle.py
commands.expected: Prints consumer predictions for activation and rollback, rejected-transition invariants, tombstones and rollback eligibility. No service or external registry is required.

content.output: Consumer predictions at x=1: A before B activation = 3.0; B after activation = 3.4; A after rollback = 3.0. Caller-version/bundle mismatch is rejected. Replacing C’s disk artifact with slope 99 or corrupting its cached artifact is rejected before prediction; pointer and cache remain unchanged. Stale, expired, wrong-target and retired-target attempts also preserve selection and output. Active/fallback retirement is rejected; after clearing fallback, A and B are tombstoned and retired activation/rollback are denied. Audit entries bind actions to actor and exact bundle hash.
content.exercise: With C selected, try activating C with B’s valid bundle and approval. Then replace C’s artifact file with slope 99 and force a consumer reload. Finally corrupt the cache entry. Verify every rejection happens before prediction and preserves pointer and cache state. Explain how this differs from rollback to a retired target.

experiments.title: Test the exact expiry boundary without mutating a registry
experiments.prediction: An approval is issued at \(100\) and expires at \(200\). Predict whether policy verification succeeds at \(199\), \(200\) and \(201\). Which inequalities define the accepted interval?
experiments.output: The policy accepts 199 and rejects 200 and 201: [True, False, False]. No activation or registry mutation occurs in this policy-only experiment.
experiments.explanation: The validity interval is \(t_{\rm issued}\le t<t_{\rm expires}\). This isolates the time rule; the main lifecycle and exercise separately test consumer behavior and side-effect-free rejection at the registry boundary.

practice.title: Exercise approval expiry and retirement at a lifecycle boundary
practice.prompt: Start a fresh registry with A active. At exactly the B approval expiry time, reject B activation without changing A. Then activate B while its token is valid, show that neither active B nor fallback A may be retired, explicitly clear fallback, retire A, and reject its reactivation. Verify the eligible B consumer still returns its prediction.
practice.hint: The valid interval is issued_at <= now < expires_at. Clearing the fallback is an explicit transition, not an effect of a rejected retirement.
practice.explanation: Approval expiry is an exclusive boundary. A rejected transition leaves selection unchanged. Retirement is allowed only after the version is neither active nor fallback; a tombstone then prevents reuse even if an old approval is otherwise valid. These are local single-writer policy rules, not authenticated organizational approval.

inputs: The local lifecycle functions and valid A/B bundles and approval records.
outputs: Expiry-boundary and retirement rejection evidence plus an eligible B prediction.
invariants: No rejected transition mutates the active selection.
Retirement remains effective despite an otherwise valid old approval.
hints: Use times 150, 160 and the exact expiry 500.
Re-read state and consumer prediction after each attempted transition.

content.question: An approval record contains a reviewer name and a matching hash. Does that authenticate the reviewer?
options: Yes, a hash verifies the reviewer identity.
No. The fixture checks binding and expiry; trusted identity and authorization are separate requirements.
Only if the model has low validation loss.
content.explanation: This check can bind approval metadata to a particular artifact and expiry. It does not authenticate the human named as reviewer. Identity and authorization require a separate trusted mechanism; a digest alone supplies neither.
content.diagnosis: Compare the whole bundle hash and target first, then time boundaries and reviewer authority. Never bypass a rejected rollout by editing a passed flag or pointing the alias manually. Keep the rejected transition in the incident record.
takeaways: Work through approval and lifecycle decisions

visual.title: Only the reviewed release passes
visual.prediction: Should changing only the target preserve the approval?
visual.reading: The matching reviewed release is accepted. The stale-approval, expired-approval and wrong-target attempts are rejected, so the bars show \(1\) accepted transition and \(3\) blocked transitions. The execution checks that rejected attempts leave selection and consumer output unchanged.
visual.connection: Approval checks compare the exact bundle and requested version with the reviewed identity, validity period and target. The active selection also keeps bundle and artifact hashes, which lets the consumer reject changed bytes on cache and disk reload paths. Retirement later removes eligibility with tombstones while retaining bundle bytes and audit identity.
visual.alt: One matching bundle is accepted and three changed or stale release attempts are rejected.

optionFeedback: The hash can bind a statement to an artifact but does not prove who wrote it. Verify reviewer identity through a separate trusted channel.

inputs: Local A/B/C artifacts, exact bundles/approvals and lifecycle functions from the lesson.
A fresh temporary registry with C selected and a consumer cache.
outputs: Explicit rejections for C selected with B approval, disk C changed to slope 99, and a corrupted C cache entry.
Pointer/cache snapshots proving rejection has no selection or cache-write side effects.
invariants: The consumer binds version, bundle and artifact identities before prediction.
Same-shape or same-name artifacts cannot bypass the selected content hash.
Each negative case changes one cause and restores the fixture before the next.
hints: Keep the original active.json bytes and a copy of the cache before each rejected call.
Use force_reload for the disk case, then test the cached path separately.
